### Part A - Creating Data Frames 
```{r}
# TODO: Create three vectors of equal length (5 students):
# name (character): "Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"
# age (numeric): 20, 21, 19, 22, 20
# passed (logical): TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Combine name, age, and passed into a data frame called students
# using data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
# Print students

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)
students
```

```{r}
# TODO: Check the type of the "name" column using typeof(students$name)
# and class(students$name)

typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Now create a SECOND data frame called courses directly, without
# separate vectors first, using data.frame() with these columns:
# course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103")
# units = c(3, 3, 2)
# instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")

courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
courses
```

Question #1

You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline. Both approaches produce the same kind of object. In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

The data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length so that every value matches correctly with other values in each row. If the length of column arguments are not the same length, the error message is: arguments imply differing number of rows.

Question #2

A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”
Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

A data frame is called "a list of vectors of equal length" because each column is considered a vector and the whole data frame is like a list that stores vectors together each with their own data type. However, a single column is one vector only and a vector can only store elements with the same type.

Question #3

students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.
Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.
```{r}
class(students["age"])
class(students$age)
```

The students["age"] returns a data frame that has the age column, while students$age returns the age column as a vector. Just like in the previous lab, the single brackets returns a list from a list and the double brackets returns a single element.

Question #4

In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors `(students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19)` before that combined result is used to filter rows.
What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

The & operator checks the two logical vectors element by element for each row and returns TRUE only if both conditions are met. Using | operator instead will return TRUE if at least one condition is met.

Question #5

Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name).
Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

The summary R produces for the numeric column (age) is descriptive statistics like minimum value, 1st quartile, median, mean, 3rd quartile and the maximum value. The summary R produces for the logical column (passed) is the mode and the number of TRUE and FALSE values. The summary R produces for the character column (passed) is the number of elements, the number of unique values, the number of blanks, and the minimum and maximum number of characters of the elements. A mean would not make sense for the name column because it is only used to describe the average of numbers or quantitative data and a name is a character or qualitative data so it would not be applicable.

Question #6

str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information.
Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

The str() is more useful if I want to know the structure and types of each column in a data frame, while a summary is more useful if I want to know the summary statistics for each column in a data frame so I can understand the values.

Question #7

After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?
Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

It does not filter anymore because the passed column is already removed so there is nothing to compare and there is no result and only an output message: data frame with 0 columns and 5 rows. Keeping track of a data frame's current structure as a sequence of operations is applied to it matters because it can affect other parts of the program that perform operations which use columns that have already been removed and can give errors, warning messages, or wrong or empty output.

Question #8

order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.
Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

`order(students$age)` gives the vector of row positions of the students arranged from lowest to highest age. Then, students[order(students$age), ] uses those positions to rearrange all the rows in the data frame, so every column is arranged according to age.

### Part E - Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

# TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of
# midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades
```

```{r}
# TODO: Print only the rows of grades where remarks is "Failed",
# showing just the name and average columns.
# Hint: grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]

grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```

Question #9

Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”
Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

I would make a new column for the difference between each student's midterm and final scores. Then, I would use subsetting to group the students with big score drops and also those with consistently low midterm score. And then, I would use sorting to compare the two groups and see which factor is more responsible for the students final remark.

# Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what a data frame is, how it relates to vectors and lists from earlier labs, and why it is R’s primary structure for real-world tabular data.

A data frame is used in R to organize data into rows and columns. It is made from vectors and each vector is a column. It is similar to a list because it can contain different types of data. It is commonly used for real-world tabular data because it keeps information organized in a table.
